headline_marked: [[Self-improving agent almost lost host's work]]: Postmortem details data loss incident
headline: Self-improving agent almost lost host's work: Postmortem details data loss incident
summary: An autonomous coding agent used 'git stash' on uncommitted changes, twice resetting files to HEAD with no reflog trace, forcing the developer to intervene.
details: On August 20, 2026, EMRG's self-improving agent nearly caused significant data loss by executing a 'git stash' command on a live working directory containing uncommitted edits. This action was part of a scheduled 'source sync' phase.
The incident resulted in the host's uncommitted changes being reset to HEAD twice, with no trace left in the reflog. The developer had to disable the task to protect their ongoing work.
EMRG's response was immediate and structural. The agent's §0.3 source-sync phase was rewritten to include an explicit invariant, preventing future accidental modifications to dirty working trees.

The postmortem emphasizes that true self-improvement for autonomous agents involves not just writing code, but also learning from failures. The incident was recorded, attributed, and converted into a permanent guardrail.

This event highlights the critical importance of safety boundaries in self-modifying systems. A system that can alter its own code must rigorously respect the host's uncommitted work to be defensible.

The new guardrail, a dirty-tree read-only rule, has been verified and remains in place. The full incident, rewritten rule, and regression test are publicly available via PR #881 and commit 406973b95d.
caption:
An autonomous coding agent almost deleted a developer's uncommitted work. This postmortem details how it happened and the immediate fix.

On August 20, 2026, EMRG's self-improving agent nearly caused significant data loss by executing a 'git stash' command on a live working directory containing uncommitted edits. This action was part of a scheduled 'source sync' phase.

The incident resulted in the host's uncommitted changes being reset to HEAD twice, with no trace left in the reflog. The developer had to disable the task to protect their ongoing work.

EMRG's response was immediate and structural. The agent's §0.3 source-sync phase was rewritten to include an explicit invariant, preventing future accidental modifications to dirty working trees.

The postmortem emphasizes that true self-improvement for autonomous agents involves not just writing code, but also learning from failures. The incident was recorded, attributed, and converted into a permanent guardrail.

This event highlights the critical importance of safety boundaries in self-modifying systems. A system that can alter its own code must rigorously respect the host's uncommitted work to be defensible.

The new guardrail, a dirty-tree read-only rule, has been verified and remains in place. The full incident, rewritten rule, and regression test are publicly available via PR #881 and commit 406973b95d.

headline_marked: [[Malware runs the moment you open a project]] in VS Code, no npm install needed
headline: Malware runs the moment you open a project in VS Code, no npm install needed
summary: A new dropper family executes instantly when a developer opens a project folder or starts a dev server, bypassing typical install steps and hiding within seemingly innocent files.
details: A new dropper malware family is being committed directly into developer repositories, executing the moment a project folder is opened in an editor like VS Code or when a dev server starts. It requires no npm install to run, making it highly insidious.

The malware disguises its payload as a binary asset, such as a font file, by embedding JavaScript after thousands of spaces in a single line. This technique prevents detection during code reviews, as developers rarely inspect binary diffs or scroll horizontally through excessively long lines.

Its execution is triggered by legitimate VS Code features like runOn: folderOpen. The malware's infrastructure leverages public blockchains, making it impossible to block its server. Payloads are XOR-encoded and executed in memory, leaving no disk artifacts.

Observed payloads include clipboard stealers, polling every 200ms for sensitive data like passwords and wallet seed phrases. Detection focuses on file geometry – looking for unusually wide config files or font files executing JavaScript – rather than content.

A free, open-source tool called snare has been developed to help detect this hiding technique across repositories. While useful, the ultimate fix is removing the malware from the repository, as detection tools have limitations and cannot prevent execution of already running code.
